Consult Summary:
- Adult male with ~5 days of viral upper respiratory symptoms (dry hacking cough, rhinorrhea, myalgias, mild sore throat) assessed as likely viral URTI; advised symptomatic treatment and safety-netting.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Cough and "cold" symptoms.
- Timeline: Symptoms began at start of the weekend (~5 days prior to consultation); ongoing at time of visit.
- Symptom character/progression:
  - Dry, hacking cough; not productive of phlegm.
  - Runny nose, mild myalgias, intermittent headache, chills.
  - Mild sore throat; patient reports mild redness at back of throat on clinician exam.
  - No reported improvement or clear worsening noted during visit.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Patient has taken paracetamol for symptom relief.
  - Clinician recommended over-the-counter Day/Night Nurse (combination cold remedies) and stated it is acceptable with his current medications.
- Associated symptoms / ROS:
  - No shortness of breath.
  - No wheeze, no "rattly" chest sounds.
  - No hemoptysis.
  - No palpable neck glands per patient.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No fever measurement recorded.
  - No sputum production.
  - No chest pain, no acute respiratory distress reported.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus, duration approximately 5–6 years.
  - Patient monitors blood glucose at home; reports readings "within normal range" currently.
- Hypertension, on lisinopril.
- No other chronic conditions documented.

Medications:
- Metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Lisinopril — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Paracetamol (patient has taken for symptoms) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- No drug allergies documented in the transcript.

Social History:
- Not documented: occupation, living situation, smoking status, alcohol or recreational drug use.
- Notes: patient performs home blood glucose monitoring.

Family History:
- Not documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings:
  - Oropharynx: mild posterior pharyngeal erythema; no tonsillar enlargement.
  - Neck: no palpable lymphadenopathy reported by patient.
  - Respiratory: clinician reported no wheeze or abnormal chest sounds; patient breathing normally.
- If other system exams performed: Not recorded.

Investigations:
- None ordered or performed; no labs or imaging reported.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold) — most likely cause of 5-day history of rhinorrhea, sore throat with posterior erythema, myalgias and dry hacking cough, consistent with clinician assessment and DDx.

DDx Integration (brief):
- 1) Acute viral URTI — High likelihood.
  - Supporting: Rhinorrhea, myalgias, headache, mild posterior pharyngeal erythema, dry cough, short duration (~5 days), no focal chest findings.
  - Opposing: No documented fever value (absence does not exclude URTI).
- 2) Acute bronchitis — Medium likelihood.
  - Supporting: Predominant cough following URTI symptoms.
  - Opposing: No wheeze, no SOB, no productive sputum; clinician did not find chest signs.
- 3) ACE inhibitor (lisinopril)–associated cough — Low likelihood.
  - Supporting: Patient is taking lisinopril (known association).
  - Opposing: Cough onset acute and accompanied by systemic viral symptoms (myalgias, rhinorrhea, throat erythema) making infectious cause more likely.

Issue 1: Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection
- Assessment: Most likely diagnosis based on history and oropharyngeal findings; no signs of lower respiratory tract infection or clinical instability at this visit.
- Plan:
  - Symptomatic treatment: paracetamol as needed (patient already using).
  - Over-the-counter combination cold remedies (Day/Night Nurse) suggested by clinician and noted as acceptable with current medications.
  - No antibiotics prescribed.
  - Safety-netting: seek re-evaluation promptly if any of the following occur — new or worsening shortness of breath, wheeze, high fever or systemic deterioration, or if symptoms persist beyond 3 weeks.
  - No further immediate investigations required.

Issue 2: Consideration of ACE inhibitor–induced cough (lisinopril)
- Assessment: Possible but unlikely contributor to acute presentation; ACE cough typically develops over weeks–months and is not usually associated with systemic viral symptoms.
- Plan:
  - No change to antihypertensive therapy at this time.
  - If cough persists after resolution of current infectious symptoms or becomes chronic, consider evaluating for ACE inhibitor–related cough and discuss alternative antihypertensive options with primary care.

Issue 3: Chronic conditions monitoring while unwell (diabetes, hypertension)
- Assessment: Type 2 diabetes and hypertension present; patient reports home monitoring with acceptable readings.
- Plan:
  - Continue regular medications (metformin, lisinopril) unless advised otherwise.
  - Continue home blood glucose and blood pressure monitoring; contact clinician if readings worsen or symptoms suggest decompensation.
  - Clinician specifically stated Day/Night Nurse is acceptable with current medications.

General plan items:
- No prescriptions issued at this visit.
- Return or seek urgent care if red-flag symptoms develop (see safety-netting above).
- Follow-up as needed if symptoms persist or worsen.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, BP, oxygen saturation) not recorded; smoking history and social/family history not documented; medication doses/routes/frequency not documented.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified — DDx is consistent with clinician’s assessment (viral URTI favored). No conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Mostly intelligible with some conversational filler; clinician assessment and recommendations documented clearly.
